big: A family of four has one policy of ₹5 lakh. In a bad year, one hospital stay uses most of it. Then a second person falls ill. What was meant to protect the whole family has run out.

lines: Should we each have our own policy, or one for the whole family?
Both work. The better question is what happens when one big claim arrives. Let us stack a cheap extra layer on top.

alt: A bar showing a base policy paying ₹5 lakh and a super top-up paying ₹15 lakh
caps: A ₹20 lakh bill arrives. The base policy pays its ₹5 lakh.
The super top-up starts after ₹5 lakh and pays the remaining ₹15 lakh.
Its premium is low, because it pays only on big claims.
A cheap second layer can protect savings from a very large bill.

intro: Each style suits a different family.
rows: One shared sum insured, usually cheaper
Each person has their own sum insured
Extra cover that starts after a set amount
Refills the sum insured after it is used
note: Parents usually do better with their own policy, since their claims can drain a shared one.

q: A family floater of ₹10 lakh covers four people. One claim uses ₹8 lakh. What is left for the others that year?
opts: ₹10 lakh each, since each person has their own cover
₹8 lakh, since the insurer refills it for the family
₹2 lakh shared among the rest, since the sum is shared
Nothing, since a claim ends the cover for everyone
why: A floater shares one sum insured. It is not separate for each person.
Refilling is a separate feature, and it often applies only for unrelated illnesses.
The shared sum insured is reduced by the claim, so only ₹2 lakh remains for the rest.
Cover continues for the remaining balance. A claim does not end it.

q: A ₹5 lakh base policy and a ₹50 lakh super top-up with a ₹5 lakh deductible face a ₹20 lakh claim. What does the top-up pay?
opts: ₹15 lakh, the part above the deductible
₹20 lakh, since the whole bill is covered by the top-up
₹5 lakh, since that is the deductible amount set
Nothing, since the base policy has already paid its share
why: The base pays ₹5 lakh, then the top-up pays the next ₹15 lakh above it.
The top-up starts above the deductible, so it skips the first part of the bill.
₹5 lakh is only the threshold for the top-up, not what it pays out.
A top-up exists to pay after the base is used, so it still pays out.

q: Meena's parents are in their sixties. Why might an individual policy suit them better than being added to a floater?
opts: Individual policies never have waiting periods for anyone at all
Their larger claims could use up the shared sum for all
Floaters cannot include anyone above sixty years of age, ever
Individual policies always cost less than a floater does
why: Waiting periods apply to individual policies too, so that statement is wrong.
Older members claim more, and a big claim can exhaust a shared sum.
Many floaters cover older members, but the cost and shared limit make it unwise.
Individual policies are usually costlier in total, not always cheaper.

q: What does a restoration benefit do?
opts: It doubles the sum insured at renewal each and every year
It returns your premium to you if you make no claim at all
It lets you claim twice over for exactly the same hospital bill
It refills the sum insured once used, often for another illness
why: It does not double the sum insured at renewal, which is a different feature.
Returning premium is not what restoration does, so this is not a match.
A bill cannot be claimed twice. The refill applies only to new claims.
Restoration refills cover after use, usually for unrelated illnesses.

pts: A floater shares one sum insured. Individual policies give each person their own.
A super top-up is a cheap layer that pays only after a set amount.
Restoration refills the cover, often for a different illness.
